extracted.intended_audience: students and coaches preparing for mathematical olympiads (China Girls' Mathematical Olympiad); problem solvers and contest authors
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of contest problems and model solutions from the China Girls’ Mathematical Olympiad (CGMO) with commentary; aimed at presenting problem statements, solution strategies (Analysis), and formal solutions. Useful for contestants, trainers, and authors studying techniques and solution presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contest format and scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: The China Girls’ Mathematical Olympiad is held in August every year. The competition lasts for 2 days, and there are 4 problems to be completed within 4 hours each day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the structural rule for problem sets and time allocation when preparing contestants or designing the contest program; problems should be suited to a 4-hour session and a total of 8 contest hours across two days. The page also lists participating regions (e.g., Russia, Philippines, Hong Kong, Macau, mainland) and organizing committee information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem attribution (posed by)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each problem is labeled with a proposer (e.g., '(posed by Wu Weichao)', '(posed by Qian Zhanwang)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When compiling problem sets or publishing solutions, include proposer attribution. This is the standard metadata accompanying each problem in the booklet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solution presentation: Analysis followed by Solution
rubrics_metrics.description: For many problems the write-up presents an 'Analysis' section outlining the approach and heuristics, followed by a formal 'Solution'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing model solutions, first give a short analysis/plan (outline main ideas or reductions), then present a clear, rigorous solution. This helps readers see motivation and the steps required to formalize the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended/existence problem handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: 'Problem (1) is an open-ended problem. It asks whether there is an arrangement satisfying the requirement of the problem. If an arrangement exists, we must construct a concrete example (see the example we have given). If not, we will prove it. (It is usually proved by contradiction.)'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For existence questions: either provide an explicit construction (if existence) or give a rigorous impossibility proof (often by contradiction). State clearly which case holds and provide the constructive example or the contradiction-based proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standard inequalities and equality-case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions routinely invoke standard inequalities explicitly (e.g., 'By Cauchy's inequality...', 'By the AM-GM inequality...') and state equality conditions: 'The equality holds if and only if ...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When solving inequalities, identify and cite the appropriate classical inequality (Cauchy-Schwarz, AM-GM, etc.), perform the manipulation, and determine and state when equality occurs. Checking equality cases is part of a complete solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of induction and the binomial theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Several solutions rely on induction or binomial-theorem-based bounding arguments (e.g., increasing sequences, growth bounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sequences or inequalities requiring growth estimates, use mathematical induction or binomial expansion as standard tools; explicitly justify base case and inductive step when using induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary constructions and adding elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Common tactic: introduce auxiliary objects to simplify counting or symmetry arguments (examples: 'Add a virtual student A so that every seat is occupied by exactly one student.'; 'Construct a tangent line...' ; add points, extend lines, construct tangents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't hesitate to add auxiliary points, lines, or virtual elements to transform the problem into a more tractable one (invariants, symmetry, bijection). Explain why the auxiliary construction preserves or reveals the quantity of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant and exchange arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use invariants and exchange operations to simplify combinatorial arrangements: 'an exchange of two students occupying adjacent seats will not change the value of S'. 'Every student can return to his/her original seat by a finite number of such exchanges... Then S' = 0.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify conserved quantities under allowed moves (invariants). Use exchange arguments to show invariance or to reduce configurations to canonical forms; make the exchange sequence and invariance explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting via bijection, binary representation, and generating functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting arguments reduce hands/values to integer solutions or binary expansions: e.g., map hand-values to ordered quadruples (j_h, r_h, b_h, g_h) and use binary representation; or use generating functions f(x) and extract coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For combinatorial enumeration, seek bijections to well-understood integer compositions/partitions, use binary representation to encode subsets, or apply generating functions and coefficient extraction. Justify uniqueness of representation when claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric methods: cyclic quadrilaterals, tangent-secant, similarity, sine rule, projections
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry solutions use classical facts: cyclic quadrilaterals, right angles, tangent–secant theorem, sine rule, similarity of triangles, and projection-length arguments (e.g., projections of points onto lines; showing projection length independent of chosen points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When solving geometry problems, identify cyclicity, perpendicularity, and similar triangles; apply the tangent–secant theorem and sine rule where appropriate. For projection invariance, reduce to equalities of cosines and use similarity to prove independence of choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutation counting from projections (directed lines method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count distinct permutations of projected orders of points on all directed lines: reduce to directed lines through a fixed point, exclude lines perpendicular to connecting segments (these give coincident projections), count K such perpendicular lines (K < C(8,2) = 28), and show the number of distinct permutations equals 2K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For problems about orderings induced by projections, restrict to lines through a fixed point, identify exceptional directions where projections coincide (perpendiculars), partition the circle of directions around these essential lines, and count permutations arising from intervals between them. Make bijections and parity arguments explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local-constraint tiling and packing upper bounds (combinatorial geometry)
rubrics_metrics.description: To bound maximum placements (e.g., crosses on a chessboard), tile the board into subboards, derive local maxima per tile (e.g., at most two centers per 3x3), and combine to get global upper bounds; then exhibit constructions to show attainability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition the domain into manageable subregions, derive tight local constraints on placements, combine additively to get a global upper bound, and provide constructive examples to show the bound is achievable. Consider symmetry and exclusion zones created by chosen placements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard proof simplifications: WLOG, order assumptions, and reduction steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs commonly simplify by 'without loss of generality' assumptions (e.g., assume a < b < c, or fix order of variables), or by reducing to a simpler equivalent inequality or combinatorial count (e.g., 'To prove ..., we only need to prove ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use WLOG to fix ordering or to reduce symmetry once you justify that other cases are analogous. Clearly state reductions and why they do not lose generality; show equivalence between the original statement and the simplified target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy template for parameter determination problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis pattern: 'First, we try to determine the range of K. Then by assumption that K is a positive integer, we may get the values for K. Afterward, we check that K can take really these values.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For problems asking to find all parameters (integers/constants) satisfying a property: (1) derive bounds/range; (2) use integrality/other constraints to narrow candidates; (3) verify each remaining candidate with explicit examples or proofs. State each step explicitly.
